title: Banda Singh Breaks Sirhind
subtitle: When Sirhind Trembled: From Vengeance to Sovereignty
figure: Banda Singh Bahadur and Wazir Khan
era: Battle of Chappar Chiri and fall of Sirhind, May 1710 CE
moral: Memory hardens where punishment and power meet.

sources.citation: Gur Bilas Patshahi Dasvin and related 18th-century Sikh chronicles
sources.note: Sikh devotional historical tradition, hagiographic but important.

sources.citation: Banda Singh Bahadur's Deg-Tegh-Fateh coinage, c. 1710
sources.note: Material evidence for proclaimed Sikh sovereignty.

sources.citation: Ganda Singh, Life of Banda Singh Bahadur (1935); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (rev. 2008)
sources.note: Critical reconstruction using Sikh, Mughal and material evidence.

panels.shot: split composition with a low-angle view of Banda Singh Bahadur advancing through dust on one side and Wazir Khan rigid atop an elephant before Sirhind on the other

dialogue.text: In May 1710, a rebel saint and an imperial governor raced toward Chappar Chiri—and the fall of Sirhind would turn Sikh vengeance into open rule.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Banda Singh Bahadur seated cross-legged, eyes closed, with a faint superimposed memory of young boys before Sirhind's walls behind him

dialogue.text: Sikh chronicles tie this march to an older wound at Sirhind, where Guru Gobind Singh’s young sons were killed under Wazir Khan’s authority.

panels.shot: wide shot of a dusty Punjab road with a mixed host moving forward, the camera slightly above and behind Banda at the head

dialogue.text: Ganda Singh sees no vast army here, but a mixed force of devoted Sikhs, paid soldiers and irregular plunderers moving under one man’s command.

panels.shot: intercut medium shot: Banda addressing followers in a village square, and Wazir Khan reading a farman in his court

dialogue.text: Sikh sources frame Banda’s march as retribution for Sirhind, while Mughal records name it rebellion against the emperor’s order and his governor, Wazir Khan.

panels.shot: wide shot of a small fortified town under attack at dawn, seen from above; smoke rising as armed men pour in through a broken gate

dialogue.text: On the march, contemporary accounts agree, towns loyal to Sirhind were stormed and plundered, as discipline and vengeance pulled in different directions.

panels.shot: medium shot inside Wazir Khan’s audience hall, low angle on him as he gestures sharply to officers before a map

dialogue.text: In Sirhind, Wazir Khan gathered imperial contingents and allied chiefs, determined to crush the rising before it reached his walls.

panels.shot: broad landscape shot of Chappar Chiri plain at first light, two armies faintly visible assembling on opposite ridges

dialogue.text: Neither Sikh nor Mughal record gives a neutral, detailed eye-witness of this field, but both agree: here Wazir Khan met Banda Singh Bahadur in open battle.

panels.shot: low-angle close-up on Banda Singh Bahadur on horseback, sword raised, dust swirling, with a sea of faces behind him

dialogue.speaker: banda_singh_bahadur_and_wazir_khan
dialogue.text: Stand firm. Today, Sirhind will hear our answer.

panels.shot: high-angle wide shot of the battle lines clashing, with special focus on Wazir Khan atop an elephant in the center

dialogue.text: Later Mughal and Sikh narratives alike place Wazir Khan high on an elephant, the visible heart of Sirhind’s power on that field.

panels.shot: tight, dynamic mid-shot of Sikhs charging toward the elephant under a hail of arrows, camera placed at their shoulder height

dialogue.text: The chroniclers differ in detail, but converge on this: the Sikh charge drove through the imperial lines toward the governor’s mount.

panels.shot: dramatic medium shot from slightly below of Wazir Khan on the elephant as armed men reach its flanks, the moment before the killing blow

dialogue.text: In the crush and dust, Wazir Khan was brought down and killed—both traditions mark his death here as the breaking of Sirhind’s will.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Mughal line collapsing, men and elephants turning away, viewed from behind Banda’s advancing riders

dialogue.text: With their governor dead, Sirhind’s forces broke; what had begun as suppression of rebels turned into a rout on the plain of Chappar Chiri.

panels.shot: distant view of Sirhind’s walls from a rise, with smoke from Chappar Chiri still faint behind, Banda’s force approaching in the foreground

dialogue.text: After Chappar Chiri, the road lay open; Sikh and Mughal accounts agree that Banda turned at once toward the city that had long overshadowed the region.

panels.shot: wide, slightly elevated shot of Sirhind’s gate under assault, with sections of wall burning and crowds rushing inside

dialogue.text: The fall of Sirhind was swift and violent; contemporary traditions speak of a city stormed, sacked and, in large part, razed.

panels.shot: moody street-level shot inside Sirhind after the sack, with blackened buildings, toppled gateways and scattered goods

dialogue.text: Sikh sources remember Sirhind’s destruction as vengeance and justice; Mughal reports record it as the shocking ruin of a major provincial capital.

panels.shot: medium shot of Banda Singh seated outdoors with peasants kneeling before him, a landlord’s house in the background marked and guarded

dialogue.text: In the months after Sirhind’s fall, evidence points to new orders—land redistributed, some zamindari claims overturned, as Banda sought to recast power in the countryside.

panels.shot: tight overhead shot of a hammer striking a coin die, with the new coin lying beside older Mughal coins

dialogue.text: Banda Singh Bahadur’s Deg-Tegh-Fateh coins—still found today—proclaimed in metal that a new sovereignty, not just a band of raiders, now claimed the land.

panels.shot: medium shot of Banda standing at dusk on Sirhind’s ruined wall, looking toward the distance, with a faint silhouette of marching imperial forces on the horizon

dialogue.text: Yet the empire he had struck was not broken; soon, imperial forces would close in, and this first Sikh state would face relentless counter-attack.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from a commemorative pillar at Chappar Chiri, blending into a stylised map of Punjab marked with Sirhind, Chappar Chiri and later Sikh centres

dialogue.text: Chappar Chiri and the fall of Sirhind show how memory hardens where punishment and power meet, turning a single campaign into the first bold line of Sikh sovereignty on the map.
